stories.body: Perplexity introduced Teammates, agents that work for you inside its Computer product. According to Perplexity, each teammate starts from your existing Projects, skills and memory, takes on ongoing jobs, monitors work and acts when something changes without being prompted, collaborates with other teammates and can message coworkers in Slack. Each runs in its own isolated environment under Computer's existing tool and Project permissions, and you can review its work, take over the desktop or redirect it. Teammates are available now for Max subscribers on the web. The shift is from prompting an assistant in a session to handing standing jobs to agents. Aravind Srinivas posted on AI's Best that Perplexity's internal workspace already has about 10,000 teammates from the last 30 days, which he says is 20 times its headcount, with about 1,000 active yesterday; that is the company's own figure. The launch post drew about 37K views on the AI Companies: Education list and the follow ups ran on AI's Best, with replies across the AI Community lists. Watch next: whether Teammates leave the Max tier, how permissions hold up when agents act unprompted, and how rival agent products answer.

stories.body: James Evans and Glen Weyl preview a Science paper titled In the Image of Their Tools. Their claim is that institutions, not model quality, are now the binding constraint on what AI can do for society. @profjamesevans posted the preview on Robert's AI Community list and said the piece appears in Science Magazine. They argue general purpose technologies only deliver lasting gains when institutions are rebuilt around them, and that neural networks' primitives of distributed representation, attention and credit assignment should shape those institutions. This is the authors' argument in a forthcoming Science piece, not an empirical finding independently verified here. stories.body: OpenAI shipped ChatGPT Images 2.6 on Wednesday evening. The update adds animated GIFs, so a prompt or a still image can become a loop with adjustable speed and frame by frame edits. It also lets people save reference images of themselves, pets or characters and reuse them without uploading again. It is live today in ChatGPT and Codex across all tiers on web, desktop and mobile. For developers, OpenAI released two new API image models, GPT Image 2.6 Flare and Sunburst. @OpenAI said Flare can return an image in as little as six seconds and the pair runs about 50% faster than before, while Sunburst targets higher quality and steadier consistency across edits. Image markup and SVG export ship alongside. The main @OpenAI post passed 294K views, and builders like @jerrod_lew were sharing GIF tests within minutes. Why it matters: image generation is turning from a novelty into a workflow, and speed plus reusable references is what product teams need to put it inside apps. Watch API pricing for Flare and Sunburst, how Google and Midjourney answer on GIFs and consistency, and whether reference images raise new likeness and consent questions.

stories.body: METR published a review of the Risks from automated R&D section of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report, done with access to the nonpublic version. The key question was whether Anthropic had crossed its AI R&D acceleration threshold. Anthropic's report said no, and METR's best guess was also no, but METR says the public report understated how plausible it was that acceleration was above the threshold. stories.body: A KAIST team released DreamFree, an imagination free World Action Model that controls robots without generating future video, while still getting better with stronger video models and more video data. stories.headline: BAAI and Chinese lab partners introduce CausGround, a plug and play causal grounding layer for embodied planners
stories.summary: The Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, with ECNU, NPU, UCAS and CASIA, introduced CausGround, a plug and play causal interaction grounding framework for embodied planners. @BAAIBeijing said it doubles embodied planning performance with zero parameter updates, targeting t
stories.body: The Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, with ECNU, NPU, UCAS and CASIA, introduced CausGround, a plug and play causal interaction grounding framework for embodied planners. @BAAIBeijing said it doubles embodied planning performance with zero parameter updates, targeting the latency and black box limits of end to end models like Astra. The idea: planners that store experience as loose text or raw trajectories cannot separate true causal dependencies from scene clutter. CausGround reasons over causal structure while a frozen multimodal model only turns language into a goal state. BAAI reported gains over vanilla planners, SelfReVision and LookPlanGraph in simulated households and real dual arm manipulation, across six open weight backbones including Qwen3.5 and InternVL3.5. Why it matters: if causal knowledge distilled in simulation can guide real robots without retraining, planners get better without new training runs. Watch for code release and independent replication.
